Parveen: bhaiya, did you ever finish that book I gave you on your birthday?
Imran: haha. no. BUT I have a new system
Parveen: oh no 😅
Imran: seriously. I stopped trying to read an hour every night. that never happened
Imran: now it's 2 pages with morning chai. that's it
Parveen: 2 pages??
Imran: the book lives on the chai tray now. kettle goes on, book opens. no decision needed
Imran: and my phone charges in the hall so I can't scroll instead
Parveen: and it's working?
Imran: 12 days straight. most days I read 10 pages, because once it's open, why not
Parveen: ok that's actually clever
Imran: also downloaded audiobooks for the bus. 20 min each way
Parveen: proud of you 👍 now finish my book pls
Imran: page 84 🙂

qa.q: Where does Imran's book live now?
qa.a: On the chai tray.

qa.q: What does Imran's 'no decision needed' suggest he thinks went wrong before?
qa.a: He seems to think relying on willpower each night failed, so he wants reading to happen automatically with the chai rather than depend on feeling motivated.

qa.q: Which changes to Imran's setup make the habit easier?
qa.a: Shrinking it to two pages, tying it to morning chai, charging the phone in the hall and using audiobooks on the bus all remove friction.

qa.q: How does Parveen's view of Imran's plan change during the chat?
qa.a: Parveen starts off doubtful, joking 'oh no', but ends up calling it clever and feeling proud of him.

grounding: Shows a young adult shrinking a reading habit, tying it to morning chai and the commute, and removing friction instead of chasing motivation.

passage:
Siddharth had tried waking at five to exercise three times this year, and three times he had given up by the second week. Sitting on the step outside his rented room in Hoshangabad, he finally made a different plan.
Not an hour of exercise. Ten squats while the milk heated for his morning tea, because the milk heated every morning anyway. And instead of taking the tempo right to the cooperative bank, he would get off at the Sethani Ghat stop and walk the last stretch along the river. He even left his walking chappals by the door, facing out.
His colleague Pradeep, who shared the tempo, laughed. "Ten squats? That's not exercise, that's stretching."
"It's ten more than last month," Siddharth said.
By the third week he was doing twenty, and Pradeep had started getting off at Sethani Ghat too.

qa.q: Where does Siddharth get off the tempo now?
qa.a: At the Sethani Ghat stop.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth decide against waking at five again?
qa.a: He had given up three times by the second week, so he seems to believe a big plan that depends on motivation won't work for him.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Tying ten squats to heating the milk and walking from Sethani Ghat linked exercise to things he already did, and the chappals by the door removed friction.

qa.q: How does Pradeep's view of the plan change?
qa.a: Pradeep first laughs that ten squats is just stretching, but by the third week is getting off at Sethani Ghat too.

grounding: Illustrates redesigning an exercise habit into a tiny version tied to tea and the commute, with less friction, rather than relying on motivation.

passage:
In Copenhagen, Yara had tried and failed three times to read every evening. By the time she got home from the hospital, she was too tired.
Her friend Freya said, "Stop trying harder. Change the setup."
So Yara made it tiny: two pages. She tied it to her morning tea, which she never skipped. She left the book on the kitchen counter, open, right next to the kettle. Her phone stayed charging in the bedroom.
Now, while the water boiled, she read two pages. Most days she read ten. Some days, only two. But she read.
"It's not motivation," she told Freya. "It's where I put the book."

qa.q: How many pages did Yara decide to read?
qa.a: Two pages.

qa.q: How was Yara feeling after three failed attempts?
qa.a: She felt tired and discouraged, too exhausted in the evenings to keep going.

qa.q: Which changes to the setup made the habit work?
qa.a: Shrinking it to two pages, tying it to morning tea, keeping the book by the kettle and the phone in the bedroom.

qa.q: How might Freya feel hearing Yara's line about where she put the book?
qa.a: Freya is likely pleased and amused that her advice to change the setup worked.

grounding: Shows a young woman shrinking her reading habit, tying it to morning tea and removing friction instead of trying to feel more motivated.

In the hospital staff room, Jahnavi opened a tiny notebook and wrote one sentence while her lunch heated in the microwave.
"What's that?" Siddharth asked.
"My journal. I tried writing every night for a year. Never lasted. I was always too tired."
"And now?"
"Now it's one sentence. Every lunch break, while the microwave runs. The notebook lives in my lunch bag, so I can't forget it."
"One sentence? That's it?"
"That's it. Some days I write a page. But one sentence counts." The microwave pinged. "I stopped trying to feel inspired. I just changed where it happens."

qa.q: Where does Jahnavi keep the notebook?
qa.a: In her lunch bag.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling when her nightly journal never lasted?
qa.a: She felt too tired and probably discouraged, failing again and again with the old setup.

qa.q: What made Jahnavi's new setup work?
qa.a: Shrinking it to one sentence, tying it to the microwave at lunch and keeping the notebook in her lunch bag.

qa.q: What might Siddharth think about the one-sentence rule?
qa.a: Siddharth seems surprised at first, then perhaps curious to try it himself.

grounding: Shows a young worker shrinking her journal habit to one sentence tied to the lunchtime microwave, changing the setup rather than motivation.

passage:
Hi Neelam,
You asked how I finally started practising the tabla again. It wasn't willpower. I've tried willpower. It lasts a week.
This time I did three things. First, I made it tiny: five minutes. Second, I tied it to my commute. I get home at seven, drop my bag, and play before I even change. Third, I took the tabla out of its case and left it on the mat in the living room. No case, no excuse.
Some days I play for forty minutes. Some days just five. But it's been two months.
Try it with your sketching?
Samir

qa.q: How long does Samir practise at minimum?
qa.a: Five minutes.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling about willpower?
qa.a: Samir felt frustrated with willpower, which only ever lasted a week.

qa.q: Which of Samir's three changes do you think matters most, and why?
qa.a: Leaving the tabla out of its case, because removing friction makes starting almost effortless.

qa.q: How might Neelam feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Neelam may feel encouraged and curious to try the same setup with Neelam's own sketching.

grounding: Shows a young adult restarting tabla by shrinking it, tying it to the commute and removing friction, not relying on motivation.

passage: "Dolma, you asked how I finally started reading again, so here's the embarrassing truth. For a year I kept promising myself an hour every night. Every night I was too tired, and every morning I felt worse about it. Then I stopped trying to feel motivated and changed the setup instead. First, I made it tiny: one page. Just one. Second, I tied it to something I already do without fail, my morning tea on the balcony. The book now lives on the tea tray, right next to the sugar. Third, I moved the phone charger to the kitchen, so the phone isn't in my hand while the kettle boils. Some mornings it's one page. Most mornings it turns into ten. My mother laughs and says, 'Sudha, the sugar is reading more than you.' But it works."

qa.q: Where does the book live now?
qa.a: On the tea tray, right next to the sugar.

qa.q: How did Sudha feel during the year of promising an hour every night?
qa.a: Sudha felt tired every night and guilty every morning, worse each time the promise broke.

qa.q: Which change in the setup seems most useful, and why?
qa.a: Tying one page to the morning tea, because it rides on a routine Sudha never skips instead of on motivation.

qa.q: How does Sudha's mother seem to see the new habit?
qa.a: She finds it funny and affectionate, teasing that the sugar reads more, which shows she has noticed the change.

grounding: Shows a habit shrunk to a tiny version, tied to an existing tea routine and stripped of friction, working where motivation failed.
